description.text: Ignazio di Loyola was born on 23 October 1491 in the Basque town of Azpeitia, the youngest of a large family that combined military service with ecclesiastical ties.  He grew up as a knight, excelling in music, dance and chivalric tournaments, and served as a soldier in the Spanish campaigns of the early 16th century.

In 1521, while defending the city of Pamplona, he was struck in the right leg by a cannonball, a wound that left him permanently lame.  During his long convalescence he read the lives of saints and began a spiritual conversion that culminated in the founding of the Society of Jesus in 1534, an order that combined rigorous education with missionary zeal.

curiosities.text: Ignazio’s injury at Pamplona was so severe that he was left with a broken leg that never fully healed, a fact that earned him the nickname “the lame knight” in contemporary accounts.
Before establishing the Jesuits, he was briefly imprisoned by the Spanish Inquisition for 42 days because of suspicions that he was a mystic or ‘alumbrado’.
The first Jesuit college was founded by Ignazio in Messina in 1548, setting a model that would be replicated in cities across Europe and the Americas.
He was declared a saint by Pope Gregory XV in 1622, a recognition that was shared with other prominent Spanish mystics such as Teresa of Avila.
Ignazio introduced a fourth vow—absolute obedience to the Pope—into the Jesuit rule, a distinctive feature that underscored the order’s close relationship with papal authority.
